_about: Fusion research facilities for the FY14 Global Fusion Explorer. Each fact was checked against the listed sources on the date given. Not an exhaustive list. country is today's country; country_then names the state at the time when it differed (Soviet Union, West Germany). end is null when the machine still runs or its end year was not found; for a retired machine last_seen (optional) is the latest year a source shows it running.

facilities.name: ZETA
facilities.site: Atomic Energy Research Establishment, Harwell, Oxfordshire
achievements: Produced about a million neutrons per pulse in August 1957
Fusion claim of January 1958 was withdrawn in May 1958: the neutrons were not thermonuclear
Its 'quiescent' plasmas later led to the reversed field pinch concept (Taylor, 1974)
facilities.importance: ZETA was one of the first large fusion machines in the world. In 1958 it was wrongly announced as a fusion success, and the public retraction taught scientists to check their measurements very carefully. Ideas tested on ZETA, such as laser Thomson scattering, are still used today.
facilities.note: Coordinates are for the AERE Harwell site, not the exact hangar.

facilities.name: Model A
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: Showed better confinement than a simple torus (1953)
facilities.importance: Model A was Lyman Spitzer's first stellarator, a small tabletop device made of glass tubes. It showed that a twisted (figure-8) magnetic field could hold a plasma better than a simple ring. It started the stellarator line that leads to Wendelstein 7-X today.
facilities.note: End year not verified, so the year filter counts it only to start + 10. Plotted at today's PPPL site; the exact building of the 1950s machine was not verified.

facilities.name: Model B
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: B-2 was shown at the 1958 Atoms for Peace exhibition in Geneva
B-3 showed particle losses about three times worse than the Bohm estimate
facilities.importance: The Model B machines were a series of improved stellarators. They showed that plasma escaped much faster than simple theory predicted, a problem called Bohm diffusion. Understanding these losses became one of the main challenges of fusion research.
facilities.note: Years for the whole B series differ between machines (B-64 1955, B-65 1957, B-66 1958); 1954–1959 is the range given for Model B. Plotted at today's PPPL site.

facilities.name: Model C
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: Reached electron temperatures of about 400 eV (about 4.6 million K) in 1969
Converted into the Symmetric Tokamak in 1970 to test Soviet tokamak results
facilities.importance: Model C was the largest of the early Princeton stellarators. Its results stayed limited by fast plasma losses, so after the Soviet tokamak success Princeton rebuilt it as a tokamak. This moment shows how the field changed direction around 1969–1970.

facilities.name: Perhapsatron
facilities.site: Los Alamos National Laboratory, New Mexico
achievements: Showed early the instabilities that troubled the pinch concept (1950s)
facilities.importance: The Perhapsatron was an early American pinch device built from spare parts. Its name joked that it might 'perhaps' make fusion. It quickly showed that pinched plasmas are unstable, a lesson that shaped later designs.
facilities.note: The first device was built in winter 1952–53; end year not verified, so the year filter counts it only to start + 10 (Z-pinch work at Los Alamos had largely ended by 1961). Coordinates are for LANL in general.

facilities.name: Scylla I
facilities.site: Los Alamos National Laboratory, New Mexico
achievements: Ion temperatures near 15 million K in 1958: described as the first clear evidence of thermonuclear fusion in a laboratory
Successor Scylla IV (1963) reached about 80 million K
facilities.importance: Scylla was a theta-pinch, which squeezes plasma very quickly with a strong magnetic field. In 1958 it gave the first convincing evidence that laboratory plasma was hot enough for real thermonuclear reactions. Its confinement time was very short, so the line ended with Scyllac in 1977.
facilities.note: End year for Scylla I not verified, so the year filter counts it only to 1968 (start + 10). Coordinates are for LANL in general.

facilities.name: T-1
achievements: First working tokamak, began operation at the end of 1958
facilities.importance: T-1 was the first tokamak, a Soviet design that combines a strong toroidal field with a current in the plasma. Its plasma was cooled by impurities from the wall, but it proved the basic idea. Almost all large fusion machines today are tokamaks.
facilities.note: Coordinates for the Kurchatov Institute are from Russian Wikipedia.

facilities.name: T-3
achievements: Electron temperature of about 1000 eV (about 10 million K) reported in 1968
Results confirmed by a British team with laser Thomson scattering in 1969
facilities.importance: T-3 made the tokamak famous. In 1968 Soviet scientists reported temperatures far higher than other machines, and many doubted them. When a British team measured the plasma in Moscow and confirmed the result, laboratories around the world started building tokamaks.
facilities.note: Start: 1962, first operation as given by the List of fusion experiments (construction 1960; the Kurchatov Institute article gives 1960). End year not given in sources, so the year filter counts it only to 1972 (start + 10).

facilities.name: ST
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: Rebuilt from Model C in 1970 and matched Soviet tokamak performance
facilities.importance: The Symmetric Tokamak was the first American tokamak, made by rebuilding the Model C stellarator in a few months. It quickly confirmed the Soviet results and beat Model C by more than ten times. After this, the United States moved its programme to tokamaks.

facilities.name: T-10
achievements: Large Soviet tokamak used for decades, including tests for ITER
facilities.importance: T-10 was a large Soviet tokamak and one of the longest-running machines in fusion history. It was used for heating and plasma studies and later for testing equipment for ITER. Its hall is now used by the new T-15MD.

sources.title: On the Program of Russian Research in the Field of Controlled Thermonuclear Fusion (Plasma Physics Reports, 2021)
Review of Recent Experiments on the T-10 Tokamak with All Metal Wall (Sarychev et al., IAEA Fusion Energy Conference, Kyoto, 18 October 2016)

facilities.note: End year not found in the sources: a 2021 paper describes T-10 as being replaced by T-15MD. last_seen = 2015: a talk at the 2016 IAEA Fusion Energy Conference reports experiments after the limiters were replaced with tungsten ones in 2015. The year filter counts T-10 to 2015.

facilities.name: T-15
achievements: Early tokamak with superconducting magnets; first plasma 1988
Reached 1 MA plasma current
facilities.importance: T-15 was one of the first large tokamaks with superconducting magnets, which are needed for long pulses. Lack of money stopped it in 1995 after only about 100 shots. The machine was later rebuilt as T-15MD.

facilities.name: T-15MD
achievements: Physically launched on 18 May 2021
facilities.importance: T-15MD is Russia's newest large tokamak, built on the T-15 project. It uses copper coils and a divertor and is meant to support ITER work and studies of fusion-fission hybrids. It is the flagship of today's Russian magnetic fusion programme.

sources.title: On the Program of Russian Research in the Field of Controlled Thermonuclear Fusion (Plasma Physics Reports, 2021)

facilities.name: TFR
achievements: First plasma on 22 March 1973: the first French tokamak
World's most powerful tokamak until 1976, when the Princeton Large Torus passed it
Ion temperatures of 1 keV in 1974 and about 2 keV with neutral beam heating by the end of 1975
facilities.importance: TFR was France's first tokamak, built soon after the Soviet T-3 results, and for a few years the most powerful tokamak in the world. It showed that the tokamak idea worked outside the Soviet Union too. It was replaced by Tore Supra at Cadarache.
facilities.note: End: 1986 (TFR article: decommissioned in 1986); the List of fusion experiments gives 1973–1984. Coordinates are city-level for Fontenay-aux-Roses, not the exact building.

facilities.name: PLT
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: About 60 million degrees with neutral beam heating on 24 July 1978
First plasma current driven by lower-hybrid radio waves (1981)
facilities.importance: PLT showed that a tokamak can reach the temperatures a fusion reactor needs. It used neutral beams and radio waves to heat the plasma, methods that are still used today. Its results gave confidence to build the much larger TFTR.

facilities.name: PDX
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: Tested the divertor for removing heat and impurities (from 1978)
facilities.importance: PDX tested the divertor, a part of the magnetic field that guides heat and impurities away from the main plasma. It also tried different plasma shapes. Divertors are now part of every large tokamak, including ITER.
facilities.note: PDX was later rebuilt as PBX/PBX-M; those years were not verified, so they are not given as a separate entry.

facilities.name: TFTR
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: Began deuterium–tritium experiments in December 1993
10.7 MW of fusion power from a 50–50 D–T plasma (1994)
Plasma temperature of 510 million °C (1995)
facilities.importance: TFTR was the large American tokamak of the 1980s and 1990s. It was one of the first machines to use real fusion fuel, a 50–50 mix of deuterium and tritium, and it produced more than 10 MW of fusion power. It did not reach break-even, but its data helped design ITER.

facilities.name: NSTX
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: First plasma on 12 February 1999
Shut down in 2012 for the upgrade to NSTX-U
facilities.importance: NSTX was one of the two large spherical tokamaks of its time, together with MAST in the UK. A spherical tokamak is shaped more like a cored apple than a doughnut and can hold a higher plasma pressure for the same magnetic field. NSTX was rebuilt as NSTX-U.
facilities.note: End: 2012, when NSTX was shut down for the upgrade (NSTX article).

facilities.name: NSTX-U
facilities.site: Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Forrestal Campus, Plainsboro NJ
achievements: Upgrade completed in 2015, doubling magnetic field and plasma current
facilities.importance: NSTX-U was meant to be the most powerful spherical tokamak of its kind. A coil failure stopped it in 2016, and a long repair project followed. Its restart matters for testing spherical tokamaks as a route to compact power plants.
facilities.note: Status 'construction' means under repair: operations stopped in 2016 after a coil failure; as of 2026 restart was expected in 2027. Start = completion of the upgrade (2015).

facilities.name: JET
achievements: First controlled release of D–T fusion power, November 1991 (about 10% tritium, 1.7 MW peak)
16 MW peak fusion power in 1997
69 MJ of fusion energy in a single pulse in its final D–T campaign (2023, announced February 2024)
facilities.importance: JET was the largest tokamak in the world for 40 years and the only one that could use tritium during most of that time. It produced record amounts of fusion energy and tested the fuel mix, wall materials and remote handling planned for ITER. It stopped in December 2023 and is now being decommissioned.

sources.title: JET takes off to new heights in fusion performance (Nuclear Engineering International)
JET's final tritium experiments yield new fusion energy record (GOV.UK, 8 Feb 2024)
Breaking new ground: JET tokamak's latest fusion energy record (EUROfusion)

facilities.note: The 1991 experiment used a dilute fuel (about 10% tritium), not a tritium-rich mix. Sources give 69 MJ (GOV.UK) and 69.26 MJ (EUROfusion) for the 2023 record.

facilities.name: START
achievements: Reached a plasma beta of 32%, well above the earlier tokamak record of 12.6%
Non-ohmic beta of 40% in 1998
facilities.importance: START was the first full-sized spherical tokamak. It showed that this compact shape can hold a much higher plasma pressure compared with the magnetic field than a normal tokamak. Its success led to MAST and to private spherical-tokamak companies.
facilities.note: Start year: 1990 (START article, List of fusion experiments); the Culham article says 1991.

facilities.name: MAST
achievements: Confirmed the high efficiency (high beta) of spherical tokamaks
Produced 30,471 plasmas between 1999 and 2013
facilities.importance: MAST continued the START work at a larger size. It studied how to control edge instabilities and how the spherical shape behaves at high power. It was rebuilt as MAST Upgrade.

facilities.name: MAST Upgrade
achievements: First plasma on 29 October 2020
Tested the Super-X divertor, designed to cut heat loads about ten times
Fully suppressed edge-localised modes with magnetic perturbation coils (2025)
facilities.importance: MAST Upgrade tests ways to handle the intense heat that leaves a fusion plasma, especially with its Super-X divertor. These results feed into STEP, the UK's planned spherical-tokamak power plant. It is the main UK machine after JET closed.

facilities.name: JT-60
achievements: Began operation on 8 April 1985
facilities.importance: JT-60 was Japan's large tokamak and one of the 'big three' of the 1980s with JET and TFTR. It was soon rebuilt as JT-60U with a larger plasma.
facilities.note: End year 1989 is from the List of fusion experiments; the upgrade to JT-60U followed in 1991. Coordinates are for Naka city (Wikipedia), not the exact institute site. Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: JT-60U
facilities.operator: Japan Atomic Energy Research Institute / JAEA
achievements: Estimated equivalent D–T gain Q of 1.25 (1998, estimate from deuterium plasmas)
Ion temperature of 45 keV (522 million K) reported in 1996
facilities.importance: JT-60U reached some of the best plasma conditions of any tokamak, although it never used tritium. Its 'equivalent Q' above 1 is a calculation of what D–T fuel would have given, not a measured result. It ended in 2008 to make room for JT-60SA.
facilities.note: Records are claims from deuterium plasmas; the Wikipedia article notes that the 1996 temperature claim was disputed. Coordinates are for Naka city (Wikipedia), not the exact institute site. Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: JT-60SA
facilities.operator: QST (Japan) and the European Union (Fusion for Energy)
achievements: First plasma on 23 October 2023
Largest operating superconducting tokamak in the world
facilities.importance: JT-60SA is a joint project of Japan and Europe and the largest superconducting tokamak working before ITER. It tests plasma scenarios and control methods that ITER and later DEMO power plants will need. Its first plasma came after a two-year delay caused by an electrical fault.
facilities.note: Coordinates are for Naka city (Wikipedia), not the exact institute site. Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: ITER
facilities.operator: ITER Organization (China, EU, India, Japan, Russia, South Korea, United States)
achievements: Tokamak complex construction started in 2013; machine assembly began in 2020
facilities.importance: ITER is the largest fusion experiment ever built, a joint project of seven members: China, the EU, India, Japan, Russia, South Korea and the United States. It aims to produce 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of heating (Q = 10), but it will not make electricity. The 2024 baseline plans research operation from 2034 and deuterium–tritium operation from 2039.
facilities.note: Schedule is a plan (2024 baseline). ITER's own site is about 1 km NE of Tore Supra/WEST (about 43.709, 5.778); plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: Tore Supra
achievements: 6 min 30 s plasma with over 1 GJ of energy injected and extracted (December 2003)
facilities.importance: Tore Supra was one of the first large tokamaks with superconducting magnets and actively cooled walls. This let it run very long pulses, a key step towards steady-state fusion. It was rebuilt as WEST.
facilities.note: End year: 2010 (WEST article); the List of fusion experiments gives 2011.

facilities.name: WEST
achievements: First plasma in December 2016
World record plasma duration for a tokamak: 22 min 17 s (1,337 s) on 12 February 2025
facilities.importance: WEST is Tore Supra rebuilt with a tungsten divertor like ITER's. It tests how tungsten walls behave in very long plasmas. Its 2025 pulse of more than 22 minutes was the longest for any tokamak at the time.

facilities.name: Pulsator
facilities.site: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Garching
facilities.operator: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics (IPP)
achievements: IPP's first tokamak (1973–1979)
Discovered high-density operation: plasma density raised to seven times what had been possible
facilities.importance: Pulsator was a small tokamak, heated only by its own plasma current. It found a way to run tokamaks at much higher density, which brought plasmas a step closer to ignition. It began the Garching tokamak line that led to ASDEX and ASDEX Upgrade.

sources.title: Pulsator (Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics)

facilities.note: Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: ASDEX
facilities.site: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Garching
facilities.operator: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics (IPP)
achievements: Discovery of the high-confinement mode (H-mode) in 1982
facilities.importance: ASDEX discovered the H-mode, a state in which the plasma suddenly holds its heat much better. Almost all tokamak power plant designs, including ITER, now rely on the H-mode. After 1990 the machine was moved to China and used to build HL-2A.

sources.title: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics (Wikipedia)

facilities.note: Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: ASDEX Upgrade
facilities.site: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Garching
facilities.operator: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics (IPP)
achievements: First plasma on 21 March 1991
Operates with an all-tungsten first wall
facilities.importance: ASDEX Upgrade is Germany's main tokamak. It pioneered the use of tungsten walls, which ITER also uses, and studies how to control heat exhaust and edge instabilities. It is one of the most productive medium-sized tokamaks in Europe.
facilities.note: Coordinates from German Wikipedia. Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: Wendelstein 7-AS
facilities.site: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Garching
facilities.operator: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics (IPP)
achievements: First advanced stellarator with modular coils (1988)
First stellarator to reach H-mode and to use an island divertor
facilities.importance: Wendelstein 7-AS was the first stellarator with a partly optimised magnetic field made by modular, twisted coils. It confirmed the theory behind optimisation and showed that stellarators can reach tokamak-like high-confinement states. Its results led directly to Wendelstein 7-X.
facilities.note: Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: Wendelstein 7-X
facilities.site: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics, Greifswald
facilities.operator: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics (IPP)
achievements: First helium plasma on 10 December 2015; first hydrogen plasma on 3 February 2016
Energy turnover of 1.3 GJ in a long plasma (2023)
World record triple product for long plasma discharges (2025 campaign)
facilities.importance: Wendelstein 7-X is the world's largest stellarator, with superconducting coils shaped by computer optimisation. It tests whether a stellarator can confine plasma as well as a tokamak while running continuously and without large plasma currents. Its results have made stellarators a serious option for power plants.
facilities.note: Coordinates from German Wikipedia.

facilities.name: EAST
facilities.site: Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Hefei
facilities.operator: Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (Chinese Academy of Sciences)
achievements: First plasma on 28 September 2006
403-second steady-state H-mode plasma (12 April 2023)
Plasma sustained for 1,066 seconds (20 January 2025)
facilities.importance: EAST is a superconducting tokamak in Hefei that specialises in very long pulses, which a power plant needs. Its long-pulse records made China a leader in this area.
facilities.note: Coordinates from German Wikipedia. Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: BEST
facilities.site: Hefei Institutes of Physical Science, Hefei
facilities.operator: Institute of Energy, Hefei Comprehensive National Science Center
achievements: Construction began in 2023
facilities.importance: BEST is a compact superconducting tokamak being built in Hefei. It aims to reach scientific break-even (Q ≥ 1) with long deuterium–tritium pulses and to study burning plasmas. First plasma is targeted for late 2027.
facilities.note: Goals and dates are plans. Exact site not verified; plotted at the EAST point in Hefei so the map groups the Hefei devices.

facilities.name: HL-2A
achievements: First tokamak with a divertor in China (2002)
facilities.importance: HL-2A was built from the main parts of the German ASDEX tokamak. It was China's first tokamak with a divertor and trained a generation of Chinese fusion scientists. It was followed by the larger HL-3.
facilities.note: End: 2018 as given by the List of fusion experiments (2002–2018); the HL-2A article still says 2002–present, so the end year is uncertain. Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: HL-3
achievements: Commissioned on 4 December 2020
H-mode with 1 MA plasma current (reported January 2024)
Ion temperature 117 million °C and electron temperature 160 million °C (announced March 2025)
facilities.importance: HL-3 is China's largest copper-coil tokamak and an ITER satellite device. It is designed for high plasma current and high temperatures and is open to international teams. Its 'double 100 million degrees' result was a key Chinese milestone in 2025.

sources.title: China sets new records in the research of new-generation 'artificial sun' HL-3 (CNNC / China Daily)
China sets out fusion progress, collaboration opportunities (World Nuclear News)

facilities.note: Sources differ on the 2025 ion temperature (117 million °C in the March 2025 CNNC release, 120 million °C in a later WNN article). Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: KSTAR
facilities.site: Korea Institute of Fusion Energy, Yuseong-gu, Daejeon
achievements: First plasma in 2008 (15 July 2008 per German Wikipedia)
Plasma above 100 million degrees for 48 seconds (2024)
H-mode sustained for 102 seconds (2024)
facilities.importance: KSTAR is South Korea's superconducting tokamak and a partner device for ITER. It is known for holding very hot plasmas, above 100 million degrees, for tens of seconds. These long, hot pulses test the control methods a power plant will need.
facilities.note: English Wikipedia gives both June and July 2008 for first plasma. Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: LHD
facilities.site: National Institute for Fusion Science, Toki, Gifu
achievements: Experiments began on 31 March 1998
Longest sustained runs of any magnetic fusion experiment (about 48–54 minutes at low density)
Over 200,000 discharges before the programme ended on 25 December 2025
facilities.importance: LHD was a large superconducting heliotron, a type of stellarator, and for many years the biggest stellarator in the world. It showed that stellarators can run plasmas for close to an hour. Its programme ended at Christmas 2025 after 27 years.

sources.title: Completion of the LHD experimental program (NIFS)

facilities.note: Coordinates from German Wikipedia.

facilities.name: SST-1
achievements: First plasma on 20 June 2013
Repeatable plasmas up to about 500 ms with currents above 75 kA (2015)
facilities.importance: SST-1 is India's superconducting tokamak and the country's largest. It was built to study long, steady pulses and helped India become a full ITER partner. It will be followed by the planned SST-2.

sources.title: SST-1 overview (IAEA Fusion Energy Conference 2014, OV/5-5)

facilities.note: Start: first plasma 20 June 2013 (IAEA overview OV/5-5); Wikipedia's '2005–present' counts from fabrication. Current operating status not confirmed beyond Wikipedia. Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: ADITYA
achievements: India's first tokamak, commissioned in 1989
First plasma of the upgraded ADITYA-U in 2016
facilities.importance: ADITYA was India's first tokamak and started the national fusion programme. Its upgrade, ADITYA-U, has a divertor-ready shape. It is mainly used for physics studies and training.
facilities.note: Current operating status not confirmed. Plotted at the shared site point so the map can group devices at this site.

facilities.name: TCV
achievements: First plasma in November 1992
First showed that negative triangularity shaping improves confinement
Plasma shape controlled by deep reinforcement learning (with DeepMind, published February 2022)
facilities.importance: TCV can shape its plasma in more ways than almost any other tokamak. This makes it a test bed for new shapes and divertors, such as negative triangularity and the snowflake divertor. In 2022 it became the first tokamak whose plasma was steered by an AI controller.

sources.title: EPFL and DeepMind use AI to control plasmas for nuclear fusion (EPFL)

facilities.note: Coordinates are for the EPFL campus (Wikipedia), not the exact building.

facilities.name: TEXTOR
facilities.full_name: Tokamak Experiment for Technology Oriented Research
achievements: Studied plasma–wall interaction for fusion reactors (1981–2013)
facilities.importance: TEXTOR was a medium-sized tokamak focused on how the hot plasma interacts with the wall. These questions decide how long wall materials can last in a reactor. Its results supported the preparation of ITER.
facilities.note: German Wikipedia gives 1981 for start of operation and 1983 for the official inauguration. Coordinates are for the research centre.

facilities.name: FTU
achievements: Reached 1.6 MA at 8 T with average electron density above 4×10²⁰ m⁻³
facilities.importance: FTU was a compact, high-field tokamak with an 8-tesla magnetic field, much stronger than most tokamaks. It showed that strong fields allow dense plasmas in a small device, an idea now used by SPARC. It is being replaced by the DTT on the same site.

sources.title: La fusione nucleare (ENEA Open Day della Ricerca)
Overview of the FTU results (Pucella et al., Nucl. Fusion 59, 112015, 2019)

facilities.note: End year not found in the sources: an ENEA page says FTU will be dismantled to make room for DTT, and the 2019 overview reports experiments after the 2016 IAEA conference, so last_seen = 2017 (the latest year a source shows it running). Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: DTT
achievements: Construction started at the ENEA Frascati centre (about 2019)
facilities.importance: DTT is an Italian tokamak being built to test solutions for removing heat from the plasma, one of the hardest problems for future power plants. It will support the European DEMO design.

sources.title: La fusione nucleare (ENEA Open Day della Ricerca)

facilities.note: Planned first plasma about 2029 according to the List of fusion experiments (uncertain). Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: COMPASS (Culham)
achievements: First plasma in 1989 in a C-shaped (circular) vessel
Restarted with a D-shaped vessel in 1992 (COMPASS-D)
Sent to Prague in autumn 2004
facilities.importance: COMPASS was a small British tokamak built at Culham. Its D-shaped vessel gave the plasma a shape like that planned for ITER. When Culham turned to the spherical tokamak MAST, the machine was given to the Czech Republic.
facilities.note: Wikipedia gives 1989 for the first plasma and 1992–2002 for the years of operation in the UK (with the D-shaped vessel). Plotted at the shared Culham site point.

facilities.name: COMPASS
facilities.site: Institute of Plasma Physics CAS, Prague-Libeň
facilities.operator: Institute of Plasma Physics, Czech Academy of Sciences
achievements: First plasma in Prague on 9 December 2008
Last experiments on 20 August 2021
facilities.importance: COMPASS began as a British tokamak at Culham and was given a second life in Prague. With an ITER-like plasma shape it let a smaller lab do research useful for ITER. It made the Czech Republic an active fusion country.

sources.title: COMPASS tokamak in Prague had its first plasma (ITER Newsline, 12 January 2009)

facilities.note: This record is the Prague period; the Culham years are the record COMPASS (Culham). The machine was sent to Prague in autumn 2004; Wikipedia gives 2006–2021 for operation in the Czech Republic, ITER Newsline gives the first Prague plasma as 9 December 2008. Coordinates are for the Libeň district of Prague, not the exact building.

facilities.name: COMPASS-U
facilities.site: Institute of Plasma Physics CAS, Prague-Libeň
facilities.operator: Institute of Plasma Physics, Czech Academy of Sciences
achievements: Under construction in Prague as a high-magnetic-field tokamak (assembly phase 2023–2025)
facilities.importance: COMPASS-U is a new compact tokamak with a strong magnetic field and hot walls. It is designed to study heat exhaust and wall materials under conditions close to those of future reactors.
facilities.note: Project pages planned first plasma for 2025; whether it has happened could not be verified. Coordinates are district-level.

facilities.name: Globus-M2
achievements: Toroidal magnetic field raised to 0.83 T and plasma current to 0.4 MA
Energy confinement time about 270% longer than on Globus-M
facilities.importance: Globus-M2 is a compact Russian spherical tokamak, the upgrade of Globus-M from 1999. It runs at a stronger magnetic field than most devices of its size. It supports Russian plans for compact fusion neutron sources and hybrid reactors.
facilities.note: Start = first full-scale experimental campaign (2019); the first Globus-M2 plasma may be earlier.

facilities.name: TJ-II
achievements: First plasma in 1998
Tested lithium wall coatings (2008)
facilities.importance: TJ-II is Spain's main fusion device, a flexible heliac whose magnetic field can be changed during research. It studies turbulence, transport barriers and wall materials. It keeps Spain active in European stellarator research.
facilities.note: Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: STEP
facilities.site: Former West Burton A power station, Nottinghamshire
achievements: Site chosen at West Burton; detailed design phase 2025–2032
facilities.importance: STEP is the UK plan for a prototype spherical-tokamak power plant. It aims to deliver about 100 MW of net electricity and to breed its own tritium, with operation planned for about 2040. It builds on START, MAST and MAST Upgrade.
facilities.note: All dates and goals are plans.

facilities.name: DIII-D
facilities.operator: General Atomics for the US Department of Energy
achievements: Renamed and upgraded from Doublet III (first plasma 1978) in 1986
Highest plasma beta of its time (early 1980s, as Doublet III) and highest neutron rate (early 1990s)
Developed ways to suppress edge-localised modes (2000s)
facilities.importance: DIII-D is the largest tokamak operating in the United States today. Its D-shaped plasma helped create the 'advanced tokamak' idea, and many plasma shaping and control methods used by ITER were tested there. It is a national user facility for scientists from many countries.
facilities.note: Coordinates are for General Atomics headquarters (Wikipedia); the exact DIII-D building was not verified.

facilities.name: Alcator C-Mod
facilities.site: MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center, Cambridge, Massachusetts
achievements: Magnetic field up to 8 T
World record plasma pressure of 2.05 atmospheres on its last day (September 2016)
facilities.importance: Alcator C-Mod was a compact tokamak with a very strong magnetic field. Its record plasma pressure showed that high fields can make smaller fusion devices possible. The same high-field idea is behind SPARC, designed by MIT and Commonwealth Fusion Systems.

sources.title: MIT Plasma Science and Fusion Center (Wikipedia)

facilities.note: Start year: 1991 (C-Mod article); the PSFC article says 1993. Coordinates are for the PSFC.

facilities.name: HSX
achievements: Showed reduced neoclassical transport with quasi-helical symmetry (from 1999)
facilities.importance: HSX is a university stellarator built with quasi-helical symmetry, a special kind of optimised field. It showed in practice that this symmetry reduces particle losses. The idea is used in several new stellarator designs.
facilities.note: Coordinates are for the university campus.

facilities.name: SPARC
achievements: Record 20 T high-temperature superconducting magnet test (September 2021)
First of 18 toroidal field magnets placed in the SPARC building (January 2026)
facilities.importance: SPARC is a private compact tokamak using new high-temperature superconducting magnets. It aims to make more fusion energy than the heating it receives (Q > 1, design value about 11), with first operation planned for 2027. If it works, it will show that strong magnets can make fusion devices much smaller.
facilities.note: All performance figures are design goals, not results.

facilities.name: NIF
facilities.site: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, California
achievements: First fusion ignition: 3.15 MJ out from 2.05 MJ of laser energy (5 December 2022)
Record yield of 8.6 MJ from 2.08 MJ of laser energy, target gain above 4 (7 April 2025)
facilities.importance: NIF is a giant laser facility that focuses its beams on a tiny fuel capsule. In 2022 it became the first experiment to get more fusion energy out of the target than the laser energy put in. The lasers themselves still use far more electricity than the fusion output, so this is a scientific, not a practical, break-even.

sources.title: Target breakthrough enabled fusion record at NIF (LLNL)

facilities.note: Start = dedication and first large experiments (2009). Gain refers to laser energy on target, not total facility energy. Coordinates from German Wikipedia.

facilities.name: OMEGA
facilities.site: Laboratory for Laser Energetics, University of Rochester, New York
facilities.operator: Laboratory for Laser Energetics (University of Rochester)
achievements: Upgraded to 60 beams in 1995
OMEGA EP dedicated on 16 May 2008
Implosions with internal pressures above 50 gigabar (reported 2016)
facilities.importance: OMEGA is the main laser for direct-drive fusion, where the beams hit the fuel capsule directly. It is a university facility used by many students and laboratories. Its results guide experiments at NIF and designs for laser fusion power plants.
facilities.note: Start = 60-beam OMEGA (1995); a first 24-beam OMEGA was completed in 1980.

facilities.name: Z machine
facilities.site: Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, New Mexico
achievements: Plasma temperatures of over 2 billion K reported (2006)
Refurbished as ZR in 2007 (350 TW radiated power)
Used for magnetized liner inertial fusion (MagLIF) experiments
facilities.importance: Z is the world's most powerful pulsed-power machine. It sends an enormous electric current through a small target, which creates huge magnetic forces and X-rays. It studies an inertial fusion route without lasers, called MagLIF.
facilities.note: Coordinates from German Wikipedia.

facilities.name: Laser Mégajoule
facilities.site: CEA CESTA, Le Barp, near Bordeaux
achievements: Declared operational on 23 October 2014
First fusion experiment with 48 beams in October 2019
facilities.importance: Laser Mégajoule is France's large laser facility, similar in size to NIF. Its main task is research for the French nuclear deterrent, but some time is used for open science. It was designed for 176 beams, which are being added step by step.
facilities.note: Coordinates are for Le Barp commune; CESTA lies in the north of the commune, exact site not verified.

facilities.name: ST40
achievements: Plasma ion temperature above 100 million °C (March 2022)
facilities.importance: ST40 is a privately built compact spherical tokamak with a strong magnetic field. In 2022 it became the first private device to reach ion temperatures above 100 million degrees. The company aims to use high-temperature superconducting magnets in future power plants.
facilities.note: Tokamak Energy has been based at Milton Park since 2013; ST40's location there is inferred, not stated directly. Coordinates are for Milton Park.

facilities.name: Norman (C-2W)
achievements: First plasma announced in July 2017
Stable plasmas above 50 million °C reported (2021)
facilities.importance: Norman is a beam-driven field-reversed configuration, a compact plasma ring without a central column. TAE's long-term aim is fusion with hydrogen–boron fuel, which produces few neutrons. These goals are plans; a smaller follow-on device, Norm, was disclosed in 2025.
facilities.note: Current status of Norman after Norm (2025) not verified. Company-reported results. Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: Polaris
achievements: Began operating at the end of 2024
Company reported measurable D–T fusion and 150 million °C plasma (announced 13 February 2026)
facilities.importance: Polaris is a pulsed field-reversed configuration machine that merges and compresses plasma rings. Helion aims to recover electricity directly from the plasma and plans a 50 MW plant for Microsoft by 2028. Its 2024 net-electricity target was not met, so its claims should be watched carefully.

sources.title: Helion achieves new industry-first fusion energy milestones (Business Wire, 13 Feb 2026)

facilities.note: Achievements are company-reported, not independently peer-reviewed. Exact Polaris site not stated in sources. Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.

facilities.name: LM26
achievements: Announced in August 2023 as a magnetized target fusion demonstration machine
First plasma in February 2025
facilities.importance: LM26 tests magnetized target fusion, where a plasma is squeezed by a collapsing lithium liner. General Fusion aims to reach 100 million °C and conditions equivalent to scientific break-even. Financial problems in 2025 reduced its operations, so the timeline is uncertain.

sources.title: All systems go: LM26 ready to compress plasmas (General Fusion, 24 April 2025)

facilities.note: Start: first plasma in February 2025 (General Fusion). Operation was reduced in May 2025 after a funding crisis; present status not confirmed. Goals are plans. Coordinates are city-level (Wikipedia city page); the exact site could not be verified.
